sections.h2: Marion County and its layers of government
sections.html:
Marion County sits in central Indiana, and Indianapolis is both the county seat and the state capital. City and county government merged in 1970 under a plan called Unigov. Four places stayed outside it: Beech Grove, Lawrence, Southport and the town of Speedway. A few small included towns, among them Clermont, Homecroft and Williams Creek, keep limited local authority, and school and fire districts were never merged into the consolidated government.

Nine townships make up the county map. Pike, Washington and Lawrence run across the top, Wayne, Center and Warren through the middle, and Decatur, Perry and Franklin along the bottom. Which township, school district and municipality a parcel sits in decides which levies show up on the bill, so two houses a few miles apart can pay quite different amounts.

The median home here was built in 1972, which puts many houses at the age where roofs, furnaces and sewer lines need replacing. Condition is a common reason owners decide to sell as-is rather than repair.

sections.h2: What sets a Marion County property tax bill
sections.html:
No single flat rate applies. Each parcel sits in a taxing district, and the district rate is applied to the assessed value after deductions and credits. The Treasurer's "Review Tax Rates" page on indy.gov lets you look up the rate for a given year.

Three separate county offices touch the bill:

  • The Assessor sets assessed values and takes appeals.
  • The Auditor handles the homestead and other deductions. The Recorder's deed page points owners here for the standard homestead and mortgage deductions.
  • The Treasurer sends the bill, collects the money and distributes it.

Indiana changed the homestead rules in 2025. The standard homestead deduction is $40,000 for the 2026 assessment date, down from $48,000. It drops by $10,000 each year and ends with the 2030 assessment date. The supplemental deduction percentage rises over the same period, to 46 percent for taxes payable in 2027. A new supplemental homestead credit of 10 percent of the bill, up to $300, starts in 2026.

If you are selling, these changes mostly land on the buyer. A new owner files for their own homestead deduction after closing, so the bill you paid may differ from the bill they receive.

sections.h2: Offices, due dates and ways to pay
sections.html:
Marion County bills in two installments, spring and fall, and the fall installment is due November 10. Payments go to the Treasurer's Office in the City-County Building.

Owners can pay online, by phone, by mail, in person or at a bank. An account login lets you schedule recurring payments, and paperless statements are available. Before you drive downtown on or near a due date, check the Treasurer's page for holiday closings and extended hours.

sections.h2: Late penalties and the tax sale
sections.html:
Pay late but inside 30 days, with no older balance on the parcel, and the penalty is 5 percent of the unpaid tax. If the tax and penalty are still unpaid after those 30 days, the penalty becomes 10 percent.

Further behind, the parcel can go to a tax sale. Marion County puts a lien on homes with unpaid taxes and auctions that lien online each fall. To stop a parcel from being sold, the owner has to pay every unpaid tax, penalty and special assessment, any solid waste and stormwater fees, and a $325 tax sale administration fee before the cutoff the Treasurer sets for that year. The county takes cash, certified checks, cashier's checks or money orders for that payment, and refuses personal or business checks.

The Treasurer's site treats a tax sale payment plan, partial payments and paying after a sale as separate topics. Call (317) 327-4444 to find out which applies to your parcel.

File a written Form 130 with the assessing official, which in Marion County is the Assessor. The deadline is June 15 of the year the tax bill is mailed when the county sent its notice of assessment after May 1, and June 15 of the assessment year when it sent the notice earlier.

After you file, the Assessor holds an informal meeting. If that fails, the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals must hold a hearing within 180 days of the petition, and a further appeal goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131.

You may pay on the prior year's assessment while an appeal is pending, without penalty, and Indiana Code 6-1.1-15-10 supports that rule. Send the Treasurer a short written explanation with the payment. The gap is not erased, though. If the appeal fails, you owe it.

Owners hurt by recent flooding can ask for a review by submitting Form 137R, and the Assessor also lists a disaster reassessment petition among its services.

sections.h2: Taxes when you sell a Marion County house
sections.html:
Sellers owe the tax for the period they owned the house, and the title company usually settles it at closing. Indiana taxes are paid after the year they cover, so a spring or fall installment can still be open on closing day.

Gather these before you list or accept an offer:

  • The latest tax statement and the parcel number.
  • Proof that the last installment was paid, or the amount still owed.
  • Any pending Form 130 appeal, since it changes what the bill should be.
  • Your tax sale list status, which the Treasurer can confirm.

The transfer itself starts at the Assessor. Deeds and sales disclosures are stamped in Room W121 for a $10 transfer fee per parcel and $20 per sales disclosure form. The stamped deed then goes to the Recorder, where the fee is $35 per document. The Assessor asks owners to build the sales disclosure in the Properly online system.

A house with back taxes, a lien or a stalled estate can be hard to sell on the open market. Many owners in that spot sell as-is, so the unpaid amount comes out of the sale price instead of being paid up front. A cash buyer also skips the lender's appraisal and any repair list, which shortens the path to closing.

faqs.q: When is Marion County property tax due?
faqs.a: Taxes come in two installments, spring and fall, and the fall installment is due November 10. Check the Treasurer's page for the exact spring date and for holiday closings.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Marion County property tax in person?
faqs.a: Go to the Treasurer's Office in the City-County Building, 200 E. Washington St., Suite 1001, Indianapolis. Regular hours are 8 AM to 4:30 PM, Monday to Friday, and the phone is (317) 327-4444.

faqs.q: How late can I file a Marion County assessment appeal?
faqs.a: Form 130 is due June 15, in either the assessment year or the year the bill is mailed, depending on when the notice went out. Confirm which applies with the Assessor at (317) 327-4907.

faqs.q: Can I stop a Marion County tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes, before the sale. You pay all unpaid taxes, penalties, special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees and a $325 administration fee by the Treasurer's cutoff. Call the Treasurer for what applies after the sale.

faqs.q: Who stamps a deed in Marion County before it is recorded?
faqs.a: The Assessor does, in Room W121 of the City-County Building. The stamped deed then goes to the Recorder. Assessor fees are $10 per parcel and $20 for a sales disclosure when one is required.
